notes:
Need to search first.I found a lot of material on the traditional reading for most verses. I couldn't find any page from the Catholic or Orthodox sites, or anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on Job 7. I also found nothing from Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal teachers beyond Guzik, so the "different readings" are mostly older commentators disagreeing. The search limit stopped me from fetching Gill's and Ellicott's full chapters, so their notes come only from search excerpts and are partial.

**Overview**
- Guzik says Job's worst crisis is spiritual rather than physical: he feels God has abandoned him, watches him like a dangerous creature, and he would welcome death.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit's outline: Job mourns his fate with no relief in sight (vv. 1–10), claims the right to complain (v. 11), then argues directly with God from v. 12 to the end.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Bible Hub's study page says Job turns from speaking to his friends to speaking to God directly at 7:7.  — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/7.htm

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** The Hebrew word Clarke and others take as military service. The Vulgate renders it "the life of man is a warfare." So Job feels drafted into a battle he didn't choose.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit prefers "a warfare (or, a time of service)": each person has set work to do within a limited time, like a hired worker.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** Every life on earth has a set time, unlike heaven or hell, which are eternal. He also applies "warfare" to believers fighting as soldiers of Christ against sin, Satan and the world. Uncommon suffering on top of that makes death seem desirable, which is Job's argument.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/7-1.html;  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/job/7-1.html
- **Barnes:** Job brings this up to defend his wish to die; it isn't wrong to want such hard service to end.  — same URL
- **Matthew Henry:** Job is excusing something he couldn't justify, his wish for death.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-1.htm
- **Other views:** Clarke records that the Septuagint reads "a place of trial" and the Vulgate (the Latin Bible used by the Catholic Church) reads "a warfare."  The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible translates "the life of man upon earth is a warfare."  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/job/7-1.html (These are translations only; I found no Catholic commentary.)

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: a slave longs for evening to end his work. The unstated point is that Job, his life's work clearly over, may be excused for longing for death. The Hebrew word means both "work" and "wages."  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- The Geneva Bible's note: even a hired servant gets some rest, so Job in constant torment is worse off.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-1.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: "months of vanity" means months that do him no good.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): "made to possess" literally means "to be heir to," used ironically. Inheriting usually brings joy, but this is a grim inheritance.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-3.htm
- Benson: "months" rather than days shows how long and tedious the suffering is.  — same URL
- Matthew Henry: when we can't work for God, sitting quietly for Him is still accepted, and hard things should be seen as appointed for a holy purpose.  — same URL
- Gill: these months are Job's share of the troubles that come from original sin, yet allotted by his heavenly Father.  — same URL

**v. 4**
- Layman's Bible Commentary: for other workers night brings rest, but for Job its length is a horror.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/job-7.html
- Pulpit: probably physical tossing, which every bad sleeper knows; compare Deut 28:67.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: insomnia, and a skin condition that kept coming back.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit links the worms to elephantiasis but calls "clods of dust" poetic rather than medical.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik, citing Ibn Ezra: the word for "hope" (*tiqwah*) can also mean "thread." Job's days run out like a shuttle out of thread, and both meanings are intended.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit: each day drags, but his whole life seems gone in a moment. He doesn't share the hopes Eliphaz offered (5:17–27) and has no hope except death.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes: Job is now speaking to God. Life is frail and quickly gone, like a breeze (compare Ps 78:39).  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-7.htm
- Benson: if people won't listen to us, God will.  — same URL
- **Different readings of "never again see good":**
  - Gill says Job doesn't mean spiritual or eternal good, since he knew he would see his living Redeemer. 
  - Pulpit says Job is speaking only of this life and isn't addressing the afterlife. 
  - The Cambridge Bible says the dead were seen as living a dreary shadow of life, cut off from people and from God.  — same URL

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: neither friend nor enemy will see him once he is in the grave. "Thine eyes" are God's: God still watches him, a comfort that may not last, and Job is about to vanish.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: one of Job's scattered statements on the afterlife. They range from uncertainty, as here, to triumphant confidence (19:25–26).  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit: Sheol is the world of the departed. It is impossible to say whether Job thought souls stay conscious there; his belief "can only be conjectured." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Layman's Bible Commentary: Job has no hope yet of being vindicated in an afterlife.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/job-7.html

**v. 10**
- Pulpit takes this literally: the dead don't come home and pick up their old lives (compare Ps 103:16).  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Benson's application: glorified saints won't return to their household cares, nor condemned sinners to their pleasures.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-7.htm

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: Job claims the right to complain. Complaint isn't always grumbling; it can be the kind of pleading God allows (Pss 77, 142).  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- **A sterner view:** Benson says Job could have reached a better conclusion than "I will complain," and should spend his last breaths in faith and prayer.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-7.htm
- Bible Hub's study page: honest lament is permitted, and being open about pain isn't rebellion.  — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/7.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: is Job as wild as the ocean or a sea monster, that he must be hemmed in?  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-12.htm
- Barnes calls the language forceful but "scarcely less irreverent than it is forcible."  — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/7-12.html
- Matthew Henry calls Job "very peevish" here.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_007.cfm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist), quoted by Guzik:** pleading our smallness is a poor argument. God might answer that we are capable of more evil than the sea.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Job/Job-7.cfm
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes):** *tannin* can mean "whale," "dragon" or "monster of the deep." For the Hebrews it was part of God's creation (Gen 1), while pagans saw it as a power to reckon with, so the reference pushes back against pagan myth. Leviathan, Tannin and Rahab stood for the forces of chaos.  — https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=job&chapter=7&verse=12
- Keil and Delitzsch think of the Nile and the crocodile. The Cambridge Bible sees the raging sea itself as a mythic monster.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-12.htm
- Gill mentions that Jarchi (Rashi) and others take the "watch" to be Satan.  — same URL

**vv. 13–14**
- Guzik: Job can't even rest; sleep brings nightmares.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Pulpit: Job believed God sent the visions, and probably this was one way Satan was allowed to test him.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Guzik, quoting Smick: to Job, God seems to be the tormentor, but the reader knows God was working through another agent.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: Job would prefer strangling to the dreams. Pulpit rejects the idea that this refers to suicide as "very forced." "Rather than my life" literally reads "rather than my bones," i.e. a living skeleton. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Matthew Henry (cited on Bible Hub): this was weakness on Job's part. We should be content to live as long as God pleases.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/7-7.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit gives other renderings: "I am wasted away" and "I shall not live alway." "Let me alone" literally means "cease from me." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Guzik: Job is so miserable he simply asks God to leave him alone.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/

**v. 17**
- Guzik: the echo of Psalm 8 is too close to be chance (Andersen), and scholars disagree on which came first. Guzik thinks Job came first and David turned his complaint into praise.  — same URL
- F. B. Meyer, quoted by Guzik: God's care for man shows our worth, as a gem-cutter's years on one diamond do.  — same URL
- Pulpit says the idea that God is too high to care for us actually lowers God, as in the Epicurean view. "Set thine heart" expresses God's tender love. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: all of life is a test, through blessings as well as hardships, though Job was probably thinking only of the hardships.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Bible Hub's study page: God's watching feels intrusive in suffering but comforts us when joined to Christ's advocacy (Rom 8:34).  — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/7.htm

**v. 19**
- "Swallow my spittle" is a saying meaning "for one instant."  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- NET note: Job wonders whether God would look away even briefly, because the constant watching is killing him.  — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Job+7%3A12%2C19-21
- Pulpit: Job asks God to look away, not to leave him, because God leaving would be the worst disaster. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm

**v. 20 (a real disagreement)**
- **Is "I have sinned" a confession?**
  - Matthew Henry says yes: Job owns his guilt before God. People can be upright without being sinless, and the truly penitent are accepted through a Mediator.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_007.cfm
  - Pulpit calls it "not so much a confession as a concession": suppose I have sinned.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
  - The NET notes also take it as hypothetical: if he had sinned, what harm would that do to God?  — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Job+7%3A12%2C19-21
- **"Watcher of men":** In the Bible God usually watches over people to protect them, but here the sense is hostile.  — same URL
- Pulpit: "target" may mean a target for arrows or an obstacle God is knocking out of his way. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- **"Burden to myself" or "to You"?** Smick says ancient scribal tradition and the Septuagint show the original was "a burden to You." The scribes changed it out of discomfort with Job's boldness, and most translations follow the later reading.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- G. Campbell Morgan: thinking sin can't affect God is too small a view of God; human sin actually wounds Him.  — same URL

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: Job sees God as a "God of pardons" (Neh 9:17). Like his friends, he wrongly assumes his suffering is punishment and doesn't see the difference between God's punishment and His loving discipline (Heb 12, Heb 2:10).  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/7.htm
- Bible Hub's study page: even when he can't name a specific wrong, Job asks for forgiveness, so confession still matters.  — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/job/7.htm
- Guzik calls "lie down in the dust" one of Job's clearly pessimistic statements about the afterlife.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-7/
- Spurgeon: Job wasn't being punished, he was being honoured.  Andersen: God was watching "with silent compassion and admiration" until the test was over (42:8).  — same URL
